source.title_on_document: When AI Joins the Brainstorm: Impacts of Generative Language Models on Collaborative Divergent Thinking

supplement.where: No supplement or appendix is identified in the complete document. Related papers La Scala et al. (2025a, 2025b) are cited for additional system details and screenshots (p. 4, Intervention Design); they are not designated supplements.
supplement.holds: No statistics are said to be in an external supplement. References occupy pp. 14-17; the PDF has no appendix.

paper_design_summary: In a Bachelor-level course at a Swiss university, student project groups were assigned to live or round-based brainstorming, with or without a GPT-4o AI peer supplying ideas during the task (pp. 4-5, Study design and Workshop Session). The paper reports 96 consenting students and 23 groups overall, but does not state how many distinct people were analyzed for fluency, elaboration, or originality after output filtering (p. 4, Participants; pp. 6-8, creative-output analyses; p. 14, Conclusion). An additional comparison of AI-generated and human-generated ideas uses the same experiment's output pool (p. 8).

studies.label: Course-based group ideation: live versus rounds crossed with AI peer versus no AI peer

assignment.what_was_assigned: Student project groups were assigned to Live, Rounds, Live AI, or Rounds AI, crossing collaboration modality with AI-peer presence. Groups were self-organized before condition assignment, and each condition met in a separate classroom. The paper calls the experiment randomized but does not describe the randomization procedure or give allocation counts (pp. 1, 4–5).
assignment.quote: We conducted a randomized controlled experiment (N=96) with four conditions,
assignment.locator: p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Study design and Participants; p. 5, Workshop Session (groups assigned to the four conditions)
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is identified in the complete document (pp. 1-17).

arms.name: Live
arms.description: Live collaboration without an AI peer: students' ideas were shared in real time on the same collaborative ideation board (pp. 4–5).

arms.name: Rounds
arms.description: Round-based collaboration without an AI peer: students saw the group's ideas from preceding rounds; the first round had no pre-existing ideas (pp. 4–5).

arms.name: Live AI
arms.description: Live collaboration with a GPT-4o AI peer that automatically submitted one idea whenever users had submitted three ideas. AI-generated ideas were identified as such (pp. 4–5).

arms.name: Rounds AI
arms.description: Round-based collaboration with a GPT-4o AI peer generating two ideas per round. Ideas were shared between rounds, and AI-generated contributions were identified as such (pp. 4–5).

participants.exclusions: The course involved 108 students; 96 consented to research. Nonconsenting students still joined the workshop but contributed no collected research data (p. 4, Participants). No person count specifically at assignment or explicit analyzed-person denominator overall, by arm, or by creative outcome is given, so n_randomized and n_analyzed remain null. The analyzed idea pool after relevance/non-idea filtering comprises 582 ideas (p. 6), including 156 AI and 426 human ideas (p. 8); 680 ideas were initially rated (p. 7). The number of distinct human contributors retained and the treatment of people whose contributions were all filtered are not stated. The conclusion's 96 students across 23 groups is an overall experiment description; the limitations' statement that all participants were pooled concerns individual characteristics and does not establish an analyzed-person count (p. 14). The timing analysis reports 9 live and 10 round-based groups (p. 6), whereas 23 groups are described overall (pp. 4, 14). The questionnaire section reports 99 responses and 63 responses analyzed after removing unexplained yes/no answers (p. 10); these concern user experience, not creative-output scoring. These discrepancies remain unexplained and do not establish a specific number of participant exclusions or verify at least 50 people analyzed for a creative outcome.
participants.who: Bachelor-level students taking an information systems design course, enrolled in economics, data science, or sports and economics programs. They worked in self-organized project groups of up to five; the paper reports 23 groups (p. 4, Participants; p. 14, Conclusion).
participants.country: Switzerland (p. 14, Limitations: one class at a Swiss university)
participants.quote: A total of 96 students provided informed consent to participate in the research component of the workshops.
participants.locator: p. 4, Participants (108 enrolled, 96 consenting); pp. 6-8, creative-output filtering and analyses (no analyzed-person denominator); p. 6, paragraph below Figures 1-2 (group timing counts); p. 10, User Experience (questionnaire counts); p. 14, Limitations and Conclusion (pooling statement and overall experimental sample)

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI GPT-4o (p. 4, Intervention Design; p. 16, OpenAI software reference)
ai_tool.how_used: An AI peer embedded in the Graasp collaborative ideation board automatically generated initial ideas from a prompt containing the group's problem statement, other participants' ideas, and instructions to generate a new idea. Its ideas were labeled AI-generated. It could not build on an existing idea. Throughput was two ideas per round in Rounds AI and one idea per three user submissions in Live AI (p. 4, Intervention Design).

task.description: Generate short, anonymous ideas, limited to 200 characters, proposing solutions to a group-defined problem for a digital innovation prototype aligned with a United Nations Sustainable Development Goal. Students could append contributions to peers' ideas. This was the ideation stage of their ongoing coursework, not an Alternative Uses Task (pp. 4–5).
task.duration: The workshop was described as two hours, with a nominal 15-minute ideation phase followed by five minutes of voting (p. 5, Workshop Session). Actual ideation durations varied; fluency was normalized to ideas per 15 minutes (pp. 6–7).

outcomes.name: Originality of human-generated ideas with versus without an AI peer
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality was scored by two independent human raters on a seven-point scale and by the Open Creativity Scoring with Artificial Intelligence (OCSAI) model; scores were normalized to 0-1 (p. 7, Ideas' Originality). Human-rater agreement: r = .45, p < .001; rater 1 versus OCSAI: r = .57, p < .001; rater 2 versus OCSAI: r = .62, p < .001 (p. 7). Mean human score versus OCSAI: r = .70, p < .001 (p. 8, Fig. 3 and opening paragraph). These methods are variants of the same outcome. Neither the prose, equation (4), nor Fig. 4 identifies which score produces the reported condition effects or author-type comparison, so measure remains null; both human_raters and automated_score are documented, but neither is confirmed as the source of the numerical effects. The normal Bayesian model analyzes ideas, without participant or group clustering (p. 6; p. 8, equation 4). N = 426 is the retained human-idea pool, not a separately printed model denominator; arm-specific observation counts are absent (p. 8). Printed intervals are 94% Bayesian HDIs; the standardizer for the reported d effects is not given.

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.17 (HDI 94%: [-0.44, 0.10]). The paper describes no significant effect; the negative point estimate has an interval spanning zero. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Ideas' Originality, paragraph following equation (4)

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.24 (HDI 94%: [-0.51, 0.01]). The authors interpret this as slightly less original ideas with an AI peer; the printed interval nevertheless includes zero. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Ideas' Originality, paragraph following equation (4)

outcomes.name: Participant creative fluency: number of ideas per 15 minutes
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each participant's number of ideas was divided by their group's activity duration and multiplied by 15 minutes (p. 7, equation 1). The authors fitted a negative-binomial Bayesian model at participant level (pp. 6–7, equation 2); Fig. 1 shows distributions by AI presence within each collaboration mode. No arm-level participant counts or numeric means/SDs are given. The ancillary correlation of group time with idea count is retained here as a related analysis, not a separate outcome: rounds Pearson (N = 10): r(8) = 0.94, p < 0.001; live Pearson (N = 9): r(7) = -0.65, p = 0.059 (p. 6, Fig. 2 and accompanying paragraph). These N values are groups, not people. The paper explicitly did not use group-level or multilevel modeling (p. 6). Reported intervals are 94% Bayesian HDIs; the standardizer for d_agent and d_collaboration is not defined. The additional Rounds-versus-Live contrast involves only no-AI arms and does not estimate AI assistance.

contrasts.reported: d_agent = -0.61 (HDI 94%: [-1.22, -0.07]) in live collaboration. The paper labels this an effect size but does not specify its standardizer.

outcomes.name: Elaboration of participants' ideas: word count after stopword removal
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Deterministic elaboration score: the number of words in an idea after removing stopwords with NLTK and its stopword corpus (p. 7, Participants Elaboration). No listed measure code explicitly covers this plain word count, so measure is null. The codebook's automated_score category denotes a creativity scoring model, and automatic computation alone does not satisfy that definition (creativity-codebook.md, section 6, Measure table). The elaboration construct and output unit are supported. A normal Bayesian model was fitted at idea level (pp. 6-7, equation 3). The exact elaboration-model observation count is not stated. Ideas are analyzed without participant or group clustering (p. 6). Reported intervals are 94% Bayesian HDIs; the standardizer for d_agent is not defined.

outcomes.name: Originality of AI-generated versus human-generated ideas in the same experiment
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Comparison by idea author, using the same retained pool rather than an independent study. Originality was normalized to 0–1; OCSAI and two human raters are described, but the particular score source for the reported author-type comparison is not explicitly identified (pp. 7–8; see S1-O1). The human pool includes ideas from the experiment's conditions and is not described as exclusively unaided. This comparison therefore does not identify the effect of giving people AI assistance. N = 582 denotes the explicitly reported retained idea pool (p. 6), including 156 AI-generated and 426 human-generated ideas (p. 8), not people. This is a within-dataset comparison by idea author and does not add another randomized study or participant sample.

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is met: the paper explicitly describes a randomized controlled experiment (p. 1, Abstract; p. 4, Study design), with student project groups assigned to AI-peer presence/absence crossed with live/round-based sharing during ordinary coursework (p. 5, Workshop Session), supporting field_rct with team assignment. Criterion 2 is unclear: 96 is an explicit consent count (p. 4) and overall experimental sample in the abstract and conclusion (pp. 1, 14), but the paper gives no verified count of distinct people analyzed across the arms for a creative-output outcome after filtering (pp. 6-8). The statement that all participants were pooled concerns ignoring individual characteristics and does not supply that denominator (p. 14, Limitations). The timing analysis uses 9 live and 10 round-based groups (p. 6), versus 23 groups overall (pp. 4, 14); questionnaire counts of 99 responses and 63 analyzed responses concern user experience (p. 10). Neither these counts nor the 582 analyzed ideas, including 426 human and 156 AI ideas, establish at least 50 analyzed people (pp. 6-8). Criterion 3 is met: originality is rated on submitted ideas, and fluency and elaboration are computed from produced output (pp. 6-8), with AI available during production in treated groups (pp. 4-5). Changing elaboration's measure code to null does not remove its status as an output-based outcome. The embedded AI-versus-human originality contrast uses the same output pool and adds no independent participant sample. Core eligibility remains unclear pending confirmation of the analyzed-person denominator; this is not evidence that fewer than 50 people were analyzed.

one_line_finding: An AI peer reduced fluency in live brainstorming (d_agent = -0.61, 94% HDI [-1.22, -0.07]; p. 7), while originality estimates were negative with intervals spanning zero (live: -0.17 [-0.44, 0.10]; rounds: -0.24 [-0.51, 0.01]; p. 8).
open_questions: What randomization procedure was used, how many people were assigned and analyzed in each arm and each creative outcome after filtering, and were at least 50 distinct people analyzed across the arms for a creative-output outcome? The paper explicitly reports randomization and 96 consenting/overall experimental students, but supplies neither allocation counts nor a verified analyzed-person denominator (pp. 1, 4-8, 14).

How do the 99 questionnaire responses (p. 10) relate to the 96 consenting students (p. 4), and why does the group-level duration analysis use N = 9 live and N = 10 rounds groups (p. 6) when the experiment is described as 23 groups (pp. 4, 14)?

Which originality score, OCSAI, mean human ratings, or a combination, was used for the reported Bayesian condition effects and AI-versus-human comparison? Both methods and their correlations are described, but the model's score source is not explicit (pp. 7–8).

What denominator defines d_agent and d_collaboration, and can uncertainty accounting for group assignment and repeated ideas within participants be obtained? The paper provides 94% HDIs but no effect-size formula or group-adjusted analysis (pp. 5–8, 14).
Does this sample overlap with any related project paper cited on p. 4? The current PDF does not state participant reuse.
notes: Final review date: 2026-10-09. Read all 495 lines of the markdown conversion, including all references; no appendix is present. The PDF contains 17 pages, with printed and PDF page numbers matching. Checked PDF text on pp. 1, 4-10, 13-14, 16-17, extracted Table 1 with PyMuPDF, and inspected Figures 1-4 rendered in memory. All retained numerical results were checked against PDF text; no effect sizes, standard errors, or graph values were calculated. The main study remains a field RCT because the task was part of ongoing coursework; the assigned units were self-organized project groups and conditions were between groups (pp. 4-5). The randomization procedure and per-arm counts are not provided. The explicit count of 96 is a consent count and overall experimental description, not a verified analyzed-person denominator (pp. 1, 4, 14). The final form therefore leaves n_analyzed null and criterion 2 unclear. The 99 questionnaire responses and 63 analyzed qualitative responses (p. 10), and the timing-analysis counts of 9 live and 10 round-based groups (p. 6) versus 23 groups overall (pp. 4, 14), remain unexplained; no specific participant exclusion count is inferred. Three output outcomes answer with_ai: originality, fluency, and elaboration. Elaboration is a deterministic word count after stopword removal; measure is null because no current measure code explicitly covers it (p. 7; codebook section 6). The author-type originality comparison is retained as S1-O4 with question none and comparison_type ai_vs_human; it uses the same experiment's data. The no-AI Rounds-versus-Live fluency contrast is retained with comparison_type other and is not an AI-assistance estimate. Relevance ratings were used to filter ideas; no AI-condition relevance effect is reported (pp. 6-7). Co-construction is an explicit collaboration measure reported by collaboration modality, not as an isolated AI-assistance or across-people similarity effect (pp. 8-9). Its ancillary statistics are retained here: direct descendants per idea, live mean = 0.13, SD = 0.41, n_live = 356; rounds mean = 0.43, SD = 0.72, n_round = 324; one-sided Mann-Whitney U = 45686.5, p < .001; descendant count versus originality r = -.09, p = 0.03, N = 582 (p. 9, Collaboration Between Participants, paragraphs below Figures 5-6). These Ns count ideas. UEQ-S and qualitative perceptions are not scores on creative output (pp. 9-13). No across-people diversity or unassisted post-AI output outcome is reported. The printed d effects have unspecified standardizers, and the confidence_interval flag denotes the reported 94% Bayesian HDI rather than a frequentist interval. Figure 1 and Figure 4 support the printed statistics; figure_only is omitted because numerical statistics are printed in the text. Both originality condition intervals include zero, so both directions remain no_clear_difference; the authors' stronger interpretation for rounds is preserved in reported. The particular originality score underlying the condition effects and author-type comparison is not identified, so both originality measure fields remain null. Analyses are at participant level for fluency and idea level for elaboration and originality, without group-level or multilevel modeling despite assignment by group (pp. 6, 14). Their printed intervals are not confirmed cluster-adjusted precision; idea-level precision also does not account for repeated outputs per person. No supplement, preregistration, participant-data release, or analysis-code release is identified. The code_url refers to the intervention application, Collaborative Ideation (Version 3.2.0), cited as La Scala (2024), not confirmed analysis code (pp. 4, 16). No company involvement or participant overlap is disclosed; shared samples with related project papers remain unconfirmed. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the prior review history; its earlier conclusion about 96 analyzed people is superseded by the corrected study, eligibility, and final fields.

challenge_resolution.problem: S1.participants.n_analyzed = 96 treats the consent/overall experiment count as a verified analyzed-person denominator for the creative outcomes.

open_items.item: open_questions[0], randomization procedure and arm allocation counts: authors could provide the assignment sequence and allocation records. This does not currently leave criterion 1 unresolved, because the paper explicitly calls the experiment randomized and describes the assigned conditions (pp. 1, 4-5).

open_questions[0], analyzed-person denominator: authors must report the distinct people analyzed in each arm and creative outcome after filtering, confirming whether at least 50 people across the arms entered a creative-output analysis. The 96 consents do not supply this denominator; this is the unresolved part of criterion 2 (pp. 4, 6-8, 14).

open_questions[1], 99 questionnaire responses versus 96 research consents: authors could explain response accounting and linkage to consent status (pp. 4, 10). Questionnaire experience responses do not independently determine creative-output eligibility; the required output-analysis denominator is tracked separately.

open_questions[1], 9 live and 10 round-based timing groups versus 23 groups overall: authors must explain the differing group coverage and whether it reflects missing groups or people in the creative-output analyses. Participant flow linking these counts to the analyzed-person denominator would settle its implications for criterion 2 (pp. 4, 6, 14).

open_questions[2] and the unresolved reconciliation.differences entry for S1-O1.measure, also applying to S1-O4: authors could identify whether OCSAI, mean human ratings, or a combination supplied the reported condition effects and author comparison, ideally with the analysis code. Criterion 3 remains met because both documented methods score submitted output (pp. 7-8, 13).

open_questions[3], definitions of d_agent and d_collaboration and valid uncertainty: authors could provide the effect-size formulas and estimates accounting for assigned groups and repeated ideas within participants, or the linked analysis data needed to obtain them. This affects effect-size extraction and pooling, not the three screening criteria (pp. 5-8, 14).

open_questions[4], overlap with related project papers: authors could identify any reused participants or cohorts. The PDF does not establish overlap or absence of overlap; clarification prevents duplicate samples but does not change the three eligibility criteria for this study (p. 4; related references on pp. 15-16).
